relations.note: Zeus gives Talos to Europa as Crete’s guardian.
Talos is given to Europa and guards her Cretan territory.
Hephaestus manufactures or supplies Talos before giving him to Minos.

relations.myth: Medea magically causes Talos’s fatal fall
relations.note: Medea’s hostile magic bewilders Talos, who wounds his ankle and loses his ichor.

relations.myth: Medea drives Talos mad with drugs
relations.note: One variant says Medea destroys Talos by inducing madness with drugs.
Medea falsely promises immortality so she can remove Talos’s bronze nail.
Medea removes the nail sealing Talos’s vein, causing his life-giving ichor to drain.

relations.myth: Medea invokes the Keres against Talos
relations.note: Medea summons the death spirits as agents of her magical assault on Talos.

relations.myth: The Dioscuri control the collapsing Talos
relations.note: Castor supports or restrains Talos as the bronze guardian collapses.

relations.myth: The Dioscuri control the collapsing Talos
relations.note: Polydeuces accompanies Castor in physically controlling or receiving the falling Talos.
Poseidon observes Talos’s collapse without taking an active role.
Amphitrite appears beside Poseidon observing Talos’s collapse.

relations.myth: Argonautic program of the Talos krater
relations.note: Hera appears in the vase’s associated Argonautic register, not in direct interaction with Talos.

relations.myth: Argonautic program of the Talos krater
relations.note: Nike appears elsewhere in the vase ensemble without a depicted direct interaction with Talos.
A genealogical Talos, possibly distinct from the guardian, is named as Cres’s son.
A problematic genealogy makes Talos father of Hephaestus, possibly reversing the usual maker relationship.
An alternative reading makes the genealogical Talos father of Phaestus rather than Hephaestus.

relations.myth: Talos prevents the Argonauts landing on Crete
relations.note: Talos tears rocks from the cliffs and hurls them at the approaching Argonauts.
Modern scholars proposed identifying Talos with the similarly named Cretan Zeus Tallaios.
Disputed comparativists equated Talos with a Phoenician or Carthaginian bronze sacrificial deity.
Modern comparisons linked Talos’s heated embrace with reported Sardinian or Carthaginian sacrifice to Kronos.
